title: DevTools and scripts read the same page
purpose: See that the DevTools panels and automation scripts both inspect the page through one protocol.
explanation: The DevTools panels are a web app. They send commands to the running page through the DevTools Protocol and get back DOM, network, JavaScript and memory data. A Puppeteer script uses the same protocol, so a manual inspection can become an automated check.
alt: Left to right: you use the DevTools panels, and a test script uses the DevTools Protocol directly. Both go through the protocol to the browser page, which sends DOM, network, JavaScript and memory data back.

learning_check.question: Why can a check you do by hand in DevTools also run in a script?
learning_check.answer: Because the panels and a script such as Puppeteer use the same DevTools Protocol to talk to the page.

title: Network panel workflow, from recording to one request's timing
purpose: See the order of work in the Network panel: record, set loading conditions, narrow the list, then read one request.
explanation: The panel records every request while DevTools is open. You can change the cache and the network speed, then filter or search the list. You open one request to read its timing phases. When you must share the evidence, you export a HAR file, which hides cookies and authorization headers by default.
alt: Left to right flowchart of six steps: record requests, set conditions such as disable cache and throttling, filter and search, pick one request, read its Timing tab phases, and export a HAR file.

learning_check.question: Why set conditions before you read a request's timing?
learning_check.answer: Cache and throttling change the phases you see, so a first-visit slow-network run shows different timing than a cached fast run.

title: From live metrics to a long task in the Performance panel
purpose: Learn the order of steps: spot a problem in live metrics, record a trace, find the long task in the flame chart, then name its cost.
explanation: The Performance panel starts with live Core Web Vitals. When a problem repeats, you record a trace. In the Main track, the flame chart shows tasks over time. The part of a task beyond 50 ms is shaded red. Bottom-up and Call tree then show which activity used the time.
alt: Flowchart: live metrics lead to recording a trace, then to the flame chart in the Main track. A decision asks whether a task exceeds 50 ms. If yes, the red part marks a long task and Bottom-up finds the cost. If no, look at other tracks.

learning_check.question: A task takes 400 ms. How much of it is shaded red?
learning_check.answer: The part beyond the first 50 ms, so about 350 ms.

title: How a source map turns generated code positions into original positions
purpose: Show the order of steps from a generated file to an original source position.
explanation: The generated file points to a map file. The tool fetches the JSON and splits the mappings string into lines and segments. It decodes each segment from base64 VLQ and adds the numbers to the previous values. The result is an original file, line and column.
alt: Flowchart with seven steps: the generated file ends with a sourceMappingURL comment, the tool fetches the map JSON, splits mappings on semicolons into lines, splits each line on commas into segments, decodes VLQ fields, adds them to the previous values, and gets an original file, line and column.

learning_check.question: Why must a tool decode segments in order instead of reading one segment alone?
learning_check.answer: Most fields are relative to the previous segment, so each value depends on the ones before it.

title: Connecting desktop Firefox DevTools to a phone over USB
purpose: Learn the order of steps that attach desktop DevTools to a tab on an Android phone.
explanation: You switch on USB debugging on the phone and in Firefox for Android, plug in the cable, and refresh the device list in about:debugging. After you accept the prompt on the phone and click Connect, the device and its tabs appear. Inspect attaches desktop DevTools to a tab.
alt: Flowchart of seven steps: turn on Developer options and USB debugging on the phone, enable Remote Debugging via USB in Firefox for Android, plug in the cable, turn on USB support in about:debugging and refresh the device list, accept the authorization prompt on the phone, then Connect and Inspect a tab.

learning_check.question: What must you do on the phone after the cable is connected and the device list is refreshed?
learning_check.answer: Accept the authorization prompt, then click Connect in about:debugging.

title: Lighthouse module map
purpose: See the four slices of Lighthouse and which one feeds which.
explanation: Lighthouse drives Chrome first, then saves raw data as artifacts, then computes metrics from the trace, then audits score the artifacts. Audits never talk to Chrome. Each arrow in the picture is one hand-off of data.
alt: Left to right flowchart: CDP session and navigation sends raw events to gatherers; gatherers send artifacts to runner and audits and a trace to metrics; metrics send values to audits; audits produce the result object.

learning_check.question: Which module talks to Chrome, and which modules never do?
learning_check.answer: Only the CDP session and navigation module talks to Chrome; gatherers read its events, and metrics and audits only read saved artifacts.

title: One Lighthouse run, from URL to score
purpose: Follow one page load from the first CDP connection to a category score.
explanation: The navigation runner connects a driver, prepares the page, and runs five instrumentation phases around the load. Gatherers record raw events and return artifacts. The runner hands each audit only the artifacts it declared, and the scoring code takes a weighted mean.
alt: Sequence diagram: navigation-runner connects and prepares the driver, gatherers record raw events, getArtifact returns artifacts to the runner, the runner passes declared artifacts to a metric audit, which returns a score, and the runner computes the weighted category mean.

learning_check.question: Why can the audit phase run later without a browser?
learning_check.answer: Because gatherers saved raw events as artifacts, and audits read only those artifacts.

title: DevTools frontend: four modules between the browser and the panels
purpose: See which module turns raw browser data into what a panel shows.
explanation: The browser sends JSON protocol messages. The protocol client routes them. Network code turns events into requests and timing bars. Source map code maps built code back to your files. Trace code turns recorded events into a model for the Performance panel. Panels only draw the results.
alt: Left to right: the browser sends protocol JSON to the protocol-client module, which feeds network-timing and source-maps. Trace events go to trace-processing. All three modules feed the panels, which draw the results.

learning_check.question: Which module owns the work of turning Network events into timing bars?
learning_check.answer: The network-timing module, after the protocol client routes the events to it.

title: One network event from the browser to a timing bar
purpose: Follow one request through the real classes, from a protocol message to its phase ranges.
explanation: The browser sends a JSON event. The connection passes it to the router. The router picks the target by session id. The network dispatcher updates the request and the log announces it. Later, the timing function turns the browser's timing numbers into named phases.
alt: Sequence of six participants: browser, connection, session router, network dispatcher, network log and the time-range function. Events flow down the chain; the log asks the function for phase ranges and gets them back.

learning_check.question: Which object chooses the target that receives an event?
learning_check.answer: The SessionRouter, using the sessionId in the event.

title: Which DevTools panel to open first for a symptom
purpose: Pick the first panel from the symptom, so the first evidence you collect can explain the problem.
explanation: Each panel records one kind of evidence. Network records requests and their timing. Performance records main-thread tasks. Memory records the heap. Elements shows the DOM and the CSS rules. Application shows service workers and storage. A phone-only error needs DevTools attached to the real device.
alt: Decision diagram: one question, what does the user report, branches to six panels. Slow first load goes to Network, slow clicks to Performance, growing memory to Memory, broken layout to Elements, old data after a deploy to Application, and an error only on a phone to remote debugging on the real device.

learning_check.question: A page gets slower each time a user opens and closes a dialog. Which panel do you open first?
learning_check.answer: Memory: take a heap snapshot, repeat the action, take another and compare them to find what grows.

title: Triage a production bug: which panel first?
purpose: Choose the first DevTools panel from the symptom a user reports, and see what evidence each panel gives.
explanation: Each panel records one kind of evidence, so the symptom tells you which panel can show the cause first.
alt: A user reports a problem on a live site. The deck groups six symptoms: a slow first load, slow clicks, growing memory, a broken layout, old data after a deploy and an error only on an iPhone. Each branch opens the panel that records the matching evidence, shows what to read there, and names the cost of opening the wrong panel first.

learning_check.question: A page gets slower each time a user opens and closes a dialog. Which panel do you open first, and what do you do there?
learning_check.answer: Memory: take a heap snapshot, open and close the dialog, take a second snapshot, and compare them to see what grows.

slides.notes: State the decision: DevTools has many panels, and the first one you open decides how fast you find evidence.
Name what each panel records. The symptom tells you which kind of evidence holds the cause.
Three symptoms look alike to a user: the site feels slow. Open each branch to see which panel separates them.
These three symptoms show wrong output, not slow output. Open each branch to see where the cause is recorded.
Turn the branches into one repeatable procedure that works for a symptom you have not seen before.
Tick Disable cache to load the page like a first-time visitor, pick a slow throttling preset, reload, then open the slowest request's Timing tab.
A heap snapshot shows what JavaScript holds in memory. It has no request timing, so it cannot show a slow server or a large file.
Click Record, repeat the slow click, stop. In the Main track a task over 50 ms is a long task; the part beyond 50 ms is red. Bottom-up shows which function used the time.
Network lists requests. A click handler that only runs JavaScript sends no request, so Network shows nothing slow while the main thread is busy.
The memory docs list three symptoms. Progressive slowdown suggests a leak, constant bad performance suggests bloat, and frequent pauses suggest frequent garbage collection.
Take a heap snapshot, do the action and undo it, take a second snapshot, then use the Comparison view. Detached DOM nodes are removed from the page but still referenced by JavaScript.
One snapshot shows the heap at one moment. A leak is growth, so you need two snapshots around the same action to see it.
Right-click the broken element and choose Inspect. The Styles pane lists the CSS rules that apply, shows overridden ones crossed out, and lets you edit a value to test a fix live.
Sources pauses JavaScript. When a CSS rule causes the broken layout, stepping through scripts spends time on code that is not the cause.

In Application, the Service Workers tab shows the active worker and offers Update on reload and Bypass for network. Cache Storage lists cached responses. In Network, tick Disable cache and reload to compare.
Elements shows the old value in the DOM. It does not show where the value came from, a cache, a service worker or the server.

On the iPhone, turn on Safari, Advanced, Web Inspector. On the Mac, turn on the Safari developer features, connect the cable, then pick the device in the Develop menu and read its Console and Sources.
Chrome device mode is a first-order approximation: the page still runs in desktop Chrome on your laptop. An error that comes from the phone's browser may not appear there.

title: Read the timing phases of one request
purpose: Name the seven timing phases of one request in order and say what makes each phase grow.
explanation: Read the longest phase first: it tells you where the time goes. The millisecond values in this walkthrough are example numbers, not measurements.
alt: The Network panel Timing tab splits one request into Queueing, Stalled, DNS Lookup, Initial connection, Request sent, Waiting (TTFB) and Content Download. A slow server grows Waiting, Slow 4G throttling grows Waiting and Content Download, and a repeat visit with the cache on loads the file from the browser cache.

learning_check.question: Waiting (TTFB) is long and Content Download is short. Where do you look first?
learning_check.answer: At the server: Waiting is one round trip plus server processing time, so a long Waiting with a short download points at server time.

purpose: Name the timing phases of one request in order and say which phase a slow network, a slow server or the cache changes.

learning_check.question: Which phase must finish before Request sent can start on a new HTTPS connection?
learning_check.answer: Initial connection, with its TCP handshakes and SSL negotiation. The Timing tab lists the phases in order. The request travels over the connection, so Initial connection, which covers the TCP handshakes and SSL negotiation, comes before Request sent.

title: Which DevTools panel answers which symptom
purpose: Pick the first panel to open from the symptom of a bug, instead of opening panels at random.
explanation: Each DevTools panel shows one kind of fact about the running page. Elements shows the DOM and CSS. Console shows errors and runs code. Sources pauses JavaScript. Network shows every request. Performance records the main thread. Memory takes heap snapshots. So the symptom tells you which panel to open first.
alt: One box labelled bug symptom points to six panels: looks wrong goes to Elements, error shown to Console, wrong logic to Sources, slow request to Network, janky click to Performance, and grows over time to Memory. The symptom decides the first panel.

learning_check.question: A page gets slower the longer it stays open. Which panel do you open first?
learning_check.answer: Memory, because a page that grows over time points to memory that the page never frees.

title: Triage a production bug: pick the first panel
purpose: Choose the first DevTools panel from a reported symptom and explain what evidence it gives and what a wrong first choice costs.
explanation: Choose a path through the deck and open the deep dives. Choose the first DevTools panel from a reported symptom and explain what evidence it gives and what a wrong first choice costs.

Each branch opens the panel that records the matching evidence (Network, Performance, Memory, Elements, Application or remote debugging), shows what to read there, and compares it with a tempting wrong first panel.

learning_check.question: A page loads slowly for new visitors but fast on a reload. Which panel do you open first?
learning_check.answer: Network, with Disable cache ticked, then the slow request's Timing tab. A reload can use the cache, so the first visit is slower. Disable cache repeats the first visit, and the Timing tab shows whether Waiting or Content Download used the time.

title: One Styles checkbox: computed padding and box width before and after
purpose: See how turning off the winning declaration changes the computed value and the box size.
explanation: Two rules set padding on one button. The Styles tab crosses out the losing .btn declaration. When you clear the .btn-primary checkbox, .btn wins again, computed padding-left drops from 24px to 16px and the box shrinks from 130 px to 114 px. Example numbers assume content-box sizing.
alt: Two columns compare a button before and after one Styles checkbox. Before, computed padding-left is 24px and the box is 130 px wide. After, padding-left is 16px and the box is 114 px, so the .btn-primary rule caused the extra width.

learning_check.question: Why does padding-left become 16px and not 0px when you turn off the .btn-primary padding?
learning_check.answer: The .btn rule still matches the button, so its crossed-out declaration wins the cascade again.

title: Performance panel deep dives
purpose: Go deeper into long tasks and yielding, and into the Core Web Vitals that the live metrics view and trace tracks show.
explanation: Live metrics tell you that something is slow; a trace tells you which task made it slow and why input had to wait.

One deep dive explains why the main thread blocks input and how scheduler.yield() splits work. The other shows how INP and CLS appear in a trace: the Interactions track, the Layout shifts track and the Insights tab.

learning_check.question: What is the blocking period of a 90 ms task?
learning_check.answer: 40 ms: the task time minus 50 ms.

The await pauses the function; the browser can run input first, then the function continues where it left off.

title: One slow click, recorded in a trace
purpose: See how a Performance recording shows a slow click as a long task on the main thread.

timeline.heading: Over 50 ms is a long task

title: Walk through a throttled trace
purpose: Read the flame chart and see how throttling and yielding change long tasks and input delay.
explanation: Throttling makes every task longer; yielding keeps each task short so the browser can handle input between pieces.
alt: A guided walk through one click handler. At 1x it is one 40 ms task. The flame chart shows time from left to right and the call stack from top to bottom. A 4x slowdown makes one 160 ms long task, and a second click waits 135 ms. Four yielding pieces of 40 ms remove the long task and cut the wait to 15 ms. At 6x the pieces are 60 ms and long again, so the work needs smaller pieces.

learning_check.question: Why does yielding cut the input delay without doing less work?
learning_check.answer: The main thread runs one task at a time. Short pieces end sooner, so a waiting click runs between pieces instead of after all the work.

title: console.table and console.dir on the same request data
purpose: Compare the table view of an array with the property view of one object, and choose columns for the table.
explanation: The same three API responses print in two shapes. console.table gives one row per item, so the slow 912 ms request stands out. console.dir lists each property of one item with its type. A second argument to console.table keeps only the columns you name.
alt: A runnable code editor prints three requests as a table with url and ms columns, then lists the url, status and ms properties of the 500 response, so the table compares items and dir inspects one item.

learning_check.question: You need to compare the duration of 40 requests. Which call do you use, and why?
learning_check.answer: console.table, because it puts one request per row, so you can scan one column of durations.

title: Two racing fetches make a search list stale
purpose: Show the order of events in the search race and where a conditional breakpoint pauses.
explanation: Each input event starts its own fetch. The fast react response renders first, then the slow re response renders last and overwrites the list. A conditional breakpoint with query !== input.value pauses only on the stale response, and async frames link it back to the call that started the fetch.
alt: Sequence diagram: the search box sends two input events, re and then react. onInput starts a slow fetch for re and a fast fetch for react. The react items arrive first and render Results for react. The re items arrive last; a conditional breakpoint on line 5 pauses there, the Call Stack with async frames shows onInput line 5, await getJSON and onInput line 4, and render writes the stale Results for re.

learning_check.question: Why does the conditional breakpoint pause on the re response but not on the react response?
learning_check.answer: For the re response, query is re but the box says react, so query !== input.value is true. For react they match.

title: Why a search box shows stale results
purpose: See how two racing fetches cause stale results, and why a breakpoint finds the cause faster than console.log.
explanation: Two requests can be in flight at the same time. The response that arrives last overwrites the list, even when it belongs to an old query.
alt: A user types re and then react in a search box. Each input event starts a fetch. The react response arrives first and the slow re response arrives last, so the list shows results for the old query. A breakpoint pauses the code before a line runs, so you can read the Scope, Watch and Call Stack panes instead of guessing with console.log.

learning_check.question: Why does the list show results for re when the box says react?
learning_check.answer: The re request was slower. Its response arrived after the react response and overwrote the list.

timeline.heading: Pick the breakpoint by the question

title: Breakpoint types and stepping
purpose: Choose the breakpoint type that answers your question, and choose how to step once the code is paused.
explanation: Each breakpoint type answers one question: where in the code, under which condition, on which element, on which request or after which event. Stepping then moves one line or one function at a time.
alt: A short deck asks which breakpoint to set for a bug. The main path compares line-of-code, conditional, logpoint, DOM change, XHR/fetch and event listener breakpoints, then the three stepping buttons. Two deep dives show how a conditional breakpoint catches the stale search response and how step into, over and out move through render.

learning_check.question: You want to log a value on every call without pausing and without editing the code. Which breakpoint type do you use?
learning_check.answer: A logpoint. It logs a message to the Console and does not pause.

slides.notes: Ask the learner what they know about the bug: the line, the element, the request URL or the event. The answer chooses the breakpoint type.
Reveal the types one at a time. Each one pauses on a different kind of event, so each answers a different question.
Once paused, choose how far to move. Step over skips a function that is not related to the bug; step into enters one that is; step out finishes the current function.
At every pause read Scope for local values, Watch for your own expressions and the Call Stack for how the code got there.
On line 5 a plain breakpoint pauses for the fresh react response and for the stale re response, so you resume past pauses you do not need.
Right-click the line number, choose Add conditional breakpoint and enter query !== input.value. DevTools now pauses only on the stale response.
Paused on line 5, step into moves the pause to line 8 inside render. The Call Stack now has render on top of onInput.
Step over runs line 8 and line 9 one at a time; the label then says Results for re. Step out returns to onInput on line 6.

title: Catch the search race with breakpoints
purpose: Use fetch, line and conditional breakpoints, stepping and async frames to find which response makes the list stale.
explanation: A conditional breakpoint skips the pauses you do not need. Async frames in the Call Stack show which earlier call started the code that is paused now.
alt: A fetch breakpoint pauses on line 12 each time a request to search?q= starts. A line-of-code breakpoint on line 5 pauses for both responses. A conditional breakpoint with query !== input.value pauses only on the stale re response. Step into enters render, step over runs one line, step out returns. After an await the stack holds only the resumed code; async frames link it back to the code that started the fetch.

learning_check.question: Which breakpoint pauses only on the stale response?
learning_check.answer: A conditional breakpoint on line 5 with the condition query !== input.value.

title: Debug a search race with breakpoints and async call stacks
purpose: Choose a breakpoint type, step through paused code and use async call stack frames to find which fetch makes a search box show stale results.
explanation: Watch, experiment with the simulation, step through the walkthrough, explore the deep dives and practice. Choose a breakpoint type, step through paused code and use async call stack frames to find which fetch makes a search box show stale results.
alt: An intro video shows a search box whose list shows results for an old query because two fetches race. A stepper lets the learner pause the code with a line-of-code, conditional or XHR/fetch breakpoint, step into, over and out, and compare the Call Stack with and without async frames. A guided walkthrough pauses at each breakpoint, a deck explains the breakpoint types and stepping, and a summary video connects the evidence to the fix.

learning_check.question: Both requests are in flight and the re request is slower. What does the label say at the end?
learning_check.answer: Results for re, because the slow response arrives last and overwrites the list. Each input event starts its own fetch, and both run at the same time. render runs once per response, in the order the responses arrive, so the slow re response writes the list last.

title: Pause, step and resume: the states of the Sources panel debugger
purpose: See which debugger control moves the page from running to paused, between functions, and back to running.
explanation: A breakpoint moves running code to paused. Step into enters the called function. Step out finishes it and pauses in the caller again. Resume runs until the next breakpoint. A breakpoint in a callback pauses later, and the Call Stack then links the callback to the code that scheduled it.
alt: Four states: Running, Paused in updateHeader, Paused in getName and Paused in a .then callback. A breakpoint moves Running to a paused state, Step into and Step out move between caller and callee, and Resume returns to Running, so the debugger is always either running or paused at one line.

learning_check.question: You are paused inside getName and want to get back to updateHeader without reading the rest of getName. Which control do you press?
learning_check.answer: Step out. It runs the rest of getName and pauses again in the function that called it.

title: Trace one minified position back to the original line
purpose: Follow how DevTools turns a position in minified code into a file, line and column in the code you wrote.
explanation: The minified file ends with a sourceMappingURL comment, so DevTools fetches the map. It splits the mappings string into lines and segments, decodes each base64 VLQ segment and adds it to the previous values. File names are examples; positions count from 0, as in the worked example of the ECMA-426 digest.
alt: Five boxes left to right: a position in app.min.js, its sourceMappingURL comment, the fetched app.min.js.map, the decoded segment AACS, and the original position in search.ts. Each lookup goes through the map, so a missing or stale map gives no position or a wrong one.

learning_check.question: The server stops sending app.min.js.map. Which box in the chain breaks, and what does the Sources panel show?
learning_check.answer: The fetch of the map fails, so DevTools cannot decode any segment. The Sources panel shows only the minified app.min.js.

title: One slow click on the main thread becomes a long task
purpose: See why one long task on the main thread delays the next paint after a click.
explanation: The main thread runs one task at a time. A 400 ms click handler blocks it, so DevTools marks the task with a red triangle and shades the 350 ms past the 50 ms limit. Style and layout run after it, and the next frame paints late, which raises INP.
alt: A click goes to the main thread, which runs handleClick_ for 400 ms, then style and layout, then the next frame. The trace marks 350 ms of the task red, so the paint after the click comes late.

learning_check.question: A click handler runs for 120 ms. How much of it does DevTools shade red?
learning_check.answer: 70 ms, the part past the 50 ms long-task limit.

title: The timing phases of one network request, in order
purpose: Name the Timing tab phases of one request in order and tell which side of the connection spends each one.
explanation: The Network panel Timing tab splits one request into phases. The browser waits in Queueing and Stalled, finds the server address in DNS Lookup, then opens a connection with TCP and SSL. After Request sent, Waiting (TTFB) covers one round trip plus server work. Content Download reads the response body. The long phase tells you what to fix.
alt: A sequence between Browser, DNS resolver and Server. The browser queues and stalls, asks the resolver for the IP address, opens a TCP and SSL connection to the server, sends the request, waits for the first byte, then downloads the body. Each phase depends on the one before it, so a slow early phase delays all later ones.

learning_check.question: A request shows a long Waiting (TTFB) bar and a short Content Download bar. Where do you look first?
learning_check.answer: At the server, because Waiting covers one round trip plus server processing time, while the body itself downloads quickly.

title: Where one page loses Lighthouse performance points
purpose: Show that the Lighthouse performance score is a weighted average, so the metric that loses the most weighted points is the first fix.
explanation: Bars compare each metric's weight (TBT 30, LCP 25, CLS 25, FCP 10, Speed Index 10, from core/config/default-config.js:419-424 @ 3b399f6) with the points one example page loses. The metric scores are invented for teaching. TBT loses 19.5 points, so splitting a long task helps most; CLS can add at most 1.3.
alt: A bar chart pairs each metric's weight with the points it loses on an example page: TBT loses 19.5 of 30, LCP 11.3 of 25, CLS 1.3 of 25, so fixing TBT moves the score most.

learning_check.question: A page has a perfect CLS score and a TBT score of 0.35. Which metric should you work on first, and why?
learning_check.answer: TBT, because it has the largest weight (30) and loses about 19.5 points, while CLS loses nothing.

title: Retainer paths that keep a detached #tree alive
purpose: See that an object is freed only when no path of references connects it to a GC root.
explanation: Window is a GC root. After body.removeChild(treeRef), #tree is detached but still reachable through treeRef and through leafRef and #leaf. Only when the learner cuts all three paths do #tree and #leaf become collectable. The Retainers section of a heap snapshot lists these paths.
alt: An editable graph links Window to body, treeRef and leafRef; body, treeRef and #leaf link to #tree. Cutting body and treeRef from #tree still leaves the path through leafRef, so the subtree is freed only after leafRef is cut too.

learning_check.question: body.removeChild(treeRef) and treeRef = null have run. Why is #tree still in memory?
learning_check.answer: leafRef points to #leaf, and #leaf keeps a parent reference to #tree, so a path from Window still exists.

title: Which desktop inspector attaches to which phone browser
purpose: Show that each phone browser pairs with one desktop inspector, and that each pair needs switches on both ends.
explanation: Three pairs: chrome://inspect attaches to Android Chrome over USB, the Safari Develop menu on a Mac attaches to iPhone Safari by cable or Xcode wireless debugging, and Firefox about:debugging attaches to Firefox for Android over USB. Clicking a node lists its setup steps. A device that does not appear usually misses one switch or prompt.
alt: Three desktop inspectors each connect to one phone browser: chrome://inspect to Android Chrome by USB, Safari Develop menu to iPhone Safari by cable or Wi-Fi, about:debugging to Firefox Android by USB, so you pick the inspector by the phone's browser.

learning_check.question: A bug appears only in Safari on an iPhone. Which desktop tool do you open, and what must be on at both ends?
learning_check.answer: Safari's Develop menu on a Mac with Show features for web developers on, and Web Inspector on in the iPhone's Safari Advanced settings.

title: Where a page keeps data, and how long it lives
purpose: Place each store in the Application panel by what it holds and how long it keeps data.
explanation: One origin has several stores. Cookies travel to the server in the Cookie header and expire at Expires or at the end of the session. localStorage keeps key-value pairs across browser sessions. sessionStorage clears when the page session ends. IndexedDB holds databases with object stores. A service worker intercepts requests and can answer from Cache Storage.
alt: A page on one origin points to Cookies sent to the server, localStorage kept across sessions, sessionStorage kept for one page session, IndexedDB object stores, and a service worker that reads Cache Storage. The lifetime and reader decide the store.

learning_check.question: A notes app keeps thousands of notes, searched by title and body. Which store fits?
learning_check.answer: IndexedDB, because it holds databases of object stores with indexes on fields such as title and body.

title: The slow product page and where you inspect it
purpose: See which file of the practice server causes which symptom, and which DevTools panel shows it.
explanation: The browser asks server.js for the page. server.js builds the HTML in page.js, the hero image in assets.js and the reviews in reviews.js. The click handler runs processInChunks from work.js in the browser. You inspect the load in the Network panel, the click in the Performance panel, and the whole page with Lighthouse.
alt: Left to right: the browser requests the page from server.js, which uses page.js, assets.js and reviews.js. The browser runs work.js on click. A dotted line shows DevTools panels inspecting the browser.

learning_check.question: Which panel do you open first for a slow click, and which for a late image?
learning_check.answer: Performance for the slow click (find the task over 50 ms); Network for the late image (read the waterfall).

title: A late response returns to onInput
purpose: Show where a stale search response re-enters onInput and where the id check stops it.
explanation: Each key press calls onInput. The request goes to the server, which waits a random time. The response returns to onInput, which renders it only when its id matches latestId.
alt: Flow from input event to onInput, server, fake API with random delay, back to onInput, then render if the id is the latest.

learning_check.question: At which step can an old response overwrite a new one, and which check prevents it?
learning_check.answer: When the late response returns to onInput; the id === latestId check stops it.

title: How the report view leaks on every route change
purpose: See which two references keep removed DOM nodes alive after a route change.
explanation: The router unmounts the old view and clears the page. The report view still has a resize listener on window and 200 rows in the cachedNodes array, so both keep the removed rows reachable. Removing both holders lets the browser free them.
alt: A URL hash change calls router render, which unmounts the report view. The report view registers a listener on window and caches rows in cachedNodes. Dotted arrows show window and cachedNodes still holding the view's rows.

learning_check.question: Why are the rows still in memory after the router clears the page?
learning_check.answer: Because window holds the onResize listener that references them and cachedNodes holds the rows, so they stay reachable.

title: Page health inspector: layers
purpose: See which layer may depend on which, and which one talks to Chrome.
explanation: Only the infrastructure layer talks to Chrome. The analysis classes read plain data, so tests need no browser. Dependencies point toward the domain.
alt: Layered diagram: DashboardServer calls the application layer, which uses four analyzers and the domain; infrastructure classes depend on the domain, and main.js wires everything.

learning_check.question: Which layer would change if you switched from Chrome to another browser driver?
learning_check.answer: Only infrastructure: ChromeCdpDriver and its helpers.

title: Page health inspector: one inspection
purpose: Follow one URL from the dashboard to the report, including the failure path.
explanation: The use case checks the URL, asks the driver for a raw capture, saves it, and builds the report. A failed capture returns an error value that the server maps to 502.
alt: Sequence diagram: the dashboard posts a URL, the server calls the use case, the use case checks the URL and calls the driver, the driver talks to Chrome, and either an error or a report returns.

learning_check.question: Why is the capture saved before the report is built?
learning_check.answer: So an analysis bug cannot lose the evidence.

title: Page health inspector: processes and ports
purpose: Know which processes run, which ports they use, and which settings the service reads.
explanation: One Node process serves HTTP and starts a headless Chrome child on demand. Chrome offers a debug WebSocket on a random local port. Reports are saved as JSON in captures/.
alt: Deployment diagram: a team browser reaches the Node process on port 3000; Node spawns headless Chrome, writes capture files, and reads its settings from environment variables.

learning_check.question: Which setting stops the service from opening localhost pages?
learning_check.answer: ALLOW_PRIVATE_HOSTS is false by default.
